12.1: All those things which you wish to reach by a roundabout road you can have now, if you do not refuse them to yourself. And this means: if you will take no notice of all the past, and trust the future to providence, and direct the present only in keeping with piety and justice. In keeping with piety, so that you may be content with the lot assigned to you, for nature designed it for you and you for it. In keeping with justice, so that you may always speak the truth freely and without disguise, and do the things which are in accordance with law and with the worth of each. And let neither another man's wickedness stop you, nor opinion nor voice, nor yet the sensations of the poor flesh which has grown about you; for the passive part will look after this. If, then, whenever the time comes that you are near to your departure, neglecting everything else you respect only your ruling faculty and the divinity within you, and if you are afraid not because you must at some time cease to live, but because you fear never to have begun to live according to nature—then you will be a man worthy of the universe which produced you, and you will cease to be a stranger in your native land, and to wonder at things which happen daily as if they were something unexpected, and to be dependent on this or that.
12.2: God sees the minds, the ruling principles, of all men stripped of their material clothing and rind and impurities. For with his intellect alone he touches only the intelligence which has flowed and been derived from himself into these bodies. And if you too get used to doing this, you will rid yourself of much of your trouble. For he who pays no regard to the poor flesh which wraps him round will surely not trouble himself with looking after clothing and house and fame and such externals and show.
12.3:
There are three things of which you are made: a little body, a little breath, which is life, and intelligence. Of these the first two are yours, so far as it is your duty to take care of them; but the third alone is truly yours. Therefore if you will separate from yourself, that is, from your understanding, whatever others do or say, and whatever you have done or said yourself, and whatever future things trouble you because they may happen, and whatever in the body which wraps you round or in the breath, which is by nature joined with the body, is attached to you independently of your will, and whatever the external vortex flowing all around whirls round, so that the power of intellect, free from the things of fate, can live pure and free by itself, doing what is just and accepting what happens and speaking the truth: if you will separate, I say, from this ruling faculty the things which are attached to it by the impressions of sense, and the things of time to come and of time past, and will make yourself like Empedocles' sphere.

“All round and in its joyous rest reposing;”

and if you strive to live only what is really your life, that is, the present—then you will be able to pass the portion of life that remains to you, up to the time of your death, free from disturbance, nobly, and obedient to your own spirit within, the god that is within you.
12.4: I have often wondered how it is that every man loves himself more than all the rest of men, and yet values his own opinion of himself less than the opinion of others. If, then, a god or a wise teacher were to appear to a man and order him to think of nothing and plan nothing which he would not speak aloud as soon as he conceived it, he could not bear it even for a single day. So much more regard do we have for what our neighbours will think of us than for what we will think of ourselves.
12.5:
How can it be that the gods, after arranging all things well and kindly for mankind, have overlooked this alone: that some men, and very good men, men who, as we may say, have had the closest communion with the divine, and through pious acts and religious observances have been most intimate with the divine, should never exist again once they have died, but should be completely extinguished?

But if this is so, be assured that if it ought to have been otherwise, the gods would have done it. For if it were just, it would also be possible; and if it were according to nature, nature would have had it so. But because it is not so, if in fact it is not so, be convinced that it ought not to have been so: for you see even for yourself that in this inquiry you are arguing with the Deity; and we would not argue like this with the gods unless they were most excellent and most just; but if this is so, they would not have allowed anything in the ordering of the universe to be neglected unjustly and irrationally.
12.6: Practise even the things which you despair of accomplishing. For even the left hand, which is ineffective for all other things for lack of practice, holds the bridle more firmly than the right hand; for it has been practised in this.
12.7: Consider what condition, both in body and soul, a man should be in when he is overtaken by death; and consider the shortness of life, the boundless abyss of time past and future, the feebleness of all matter.
12.8: Contemplate the forming principles, the forms, of things stripped of their coverings; the purposes of actions; consider what pain is, what pleasure is, and death, and fame; who is the cause of his own unease; how no man is obstructed by another; that everything is opinion.
12.9: In applying your principles you must be like the pancratiast, not like the gladiator; for the gladiator drops the sword he uses and is killed; but the other always has his hand, and needs to do nothing other than use it.
12.10: See what things are in themselves, dividing them into matter, form, and purpose.
12.11: What power man has to do nothing except what God will approve, and to accept all that God may give him.
12.12: With regard to what happens in keeping with nature, we ought to blame neither the gods, for they do nothing wrong either willingly or unwillingly, nor men, for they do nothing wrong except unwillingly. So we should blame nobody.
12.13: How ridiculous, and what a stranger, is the man who is surprised at anything which happens in life.
12.14: Either there is a fated necessity and an unconquerable order, or a kind providence, or a confusion without a purpose and without a director. If, then, there is an unconquerable necessity, why do you resist? But if there is a providence which allows itself to be won over, make yourself worthy of help from the divine. But if there is a confusion without a governor, be content that in such a storm you have in yourself a certain ruling intelligence. And even if the storm carries you away, let it carry away the poor flesh, the poor breath, everything else; for the intelligence at least it will not carry away.
12.15: Does the light of the lamp shine without losing its brightness until it is put out? And shall the truth which is in you, and justice and self-control, be extinguished before your death?
12.16: When a man seems to have done wrong, say: How then do I know whether this is a wrongful act? And even if he has done wrong, how do I know that he has not condemned himself? And so this is like tearing his own face. Consider that he who would not have the bad man do wrong is like the man who would not have the fig tree bear juice in the figs, and infants cry, and the horse neigh, and whatever else must necessarily be. For what must a man do who has such a character? If, then, you are irritable, cure this man's disposition.
12.17: If it is not right, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it. For let your efforts be—
12.18: In everything, always observe what it is that produces an impression in you, and resolve it by dividing it into the formal, the material, the purpose, and the time within which it must end.
12.19: Realise at last that you have in you something better and more divine than the things which cause the various passions, and, as it were, pull you by the strings. What is in my mind now—is it fear, or suspicion, or desire, or anything of the kind?
12.20: First, do nothing thoughtlessly, nor without a purpose. Second, make your acts aim at nothing other than a social end.
12.21: Consider that before long you will be nobody and nowhere, nor will any of the things exist which you now see, nor any of those who are now living. For all things are formed by nature to change and be turned and to perish, so that other things may exist in continuous succession.
12.22: Consider that everything is opinion, and opinion is in your power. Take away, then, when you choose, your opinion, and like a sailor who has rounded the headland, you will find calm, everything still, and a waveless bay.
12.23: Any one activity, whatever it may be, when it has ceased at its proper time, suffers no evil because it has ceased; nor does he who has done this act suffer any evil for this reason, that the act has ceased. In the same way, then, the whole, which consists of all the acts, which is our life, if it ceases at its proper time, suffers no evil for this reason, that it has ceased; nor has he who has ended this series at the proper time been badly treated. But the proper time and the limit are fixed by nature: sometimes, as in old age, by the particular nature of man, but always by the universal nature, through the change of whose parts the whole universe stays ever young and perfect. And everything which is useful to the universal is always good and in season. Therefore the ending of life for every man is no evil, because it is not shameful, since it is both independent of the will and not opposed to the general interest; but it is good, since it is timely, and profitable to and in harmony with the universal. For in this way too he is moved by the Deity who is moved in the same way as the Deity, and moved towards the same thing in his mind.
12.24: You must have these three principles ready: In the things which you do, do nothing either thoughtlessly or otherwise than as justice herself would act; but with regard to what may happen to you from outside, consider that it happens either by chance or according to providence, and you must neither blame chance nor accuse providence. Second, consider what every being is from the seed to the time when it receives a soul, and from receiving a soul to giving it back, and of what things every being is made up, and into what things it is resolved. Third, if you were suddenly raised up above the earth, and looked down on human things, and observed how great their variety is, and at the same time saw at a glance how great is the number of beings who live all around in the air and the ether, consider that as often as you were raised up, you would see the same things: sameness of form and shortness of duration. Are these things to be proud of?
12.25: Throw away opinion: you are saved. Who, then, stops you from throwing it away?
12.26: When you are troubled about anything, you have forgotten this, that all things happen according to the universal nature; and forgotten this, that a man's wrongful act is nothing to you; and further you have forgotten this, that everything which happens always happened so and will happen so, and now happens so everywhere; forgotten this too, how close the kinship is between a man and the whole human race, for it is a community not of a little blood or seed, but of intelligence. And you have forgotten this too, that every man's intelligence is a god and flows out from the Deity; and forgotten this, that nothing is a man's own, but that his child and his body and his very soul came from the Deity; forgotten this, that everything is opinion; and lastly you have forgotten that every man lives only the present moment, and loses only this.
12.27: Constantly call to mind those who have complained greatly about anything, those who have been most conspicuous for the greatest fame or misfortunes or hostilities or fortunes of any kind: then think, where are they all now? Smoke and ash and a tale, or not even a tale. And let everything of this sort also be present to your mind: how Fabius Catellinus lived in the country, and Lucius Lupus in his gardens, and Stertinius at Briae, and Tiberius at Capreae, and Velius Rufus, or Rufus at Velia; and in short think of the eager pursuit of anything combined with pride; and how worthless everything is which men strain after so violently; and how much more philosophical it is for a man, in the opportunities given to him, to show himself just, self-controlled, obedient to the gods, and to do this with all simplicity: for the pride which is proud of its lack of pride is the most intolerable of all.
12.28: To those who ask, Where have you seen the gods, or how do you know that they exist, and so worship them, I answer, in the first place, they may be seen even with the eyes; in the second place, I have not seen even my own soul, and yet I honour it. So then with regard to the gods, from what I constantly experience of their power, from this I know that they exist, and I revere them.
12.29: The safety of life is this: to examine everything all through, what it is in itself, what is its material, what its formal part; with all your soul to do justice and to speak the truth. What remains, except to enjoy life by joining one good thing to another so as not to leave even the smallest gaps between?
12.30: There is one light of the sun, though it is broken up by walls, mountains, and countless other things. There is one common substance, though it is distributed among countless bodies which have their own qualities. There is one soul, though it is distributed among countless natures and individual boundaries, that is, individuals. There is one intelligent soul, though it seems to be divided. Now in the things which have been mentioned, all the other parts, such as those which are air and matter, are without sensation and have no fellowship with one another: and yet even these parts are held together by the intelligent principle and the gravitation towards the same. But intellect in a special way tends towards what is of its own kind, and joins with it, and the feeling for communion is not broken.
12.31: What do you want—to go on existing? Well, do you want to have sensation, movement, growth, and then again to stop growing, to use your speech, to think? Which of all these things seems to you worth desiring? But if it is easy to set little value on all these things, turn to what remains, which is to follow reason and God. But it is inconsistent with honouring reason and God to be troubled because by death a man will be deprived of the other things.
12.32: How small a part of boundless and unfathomable time is assigned to every man, for it is very soon swallowed up in eternity! And how small a part of the whole substance; and how small a part of the universal soul; and on what a small clod of the whole earth you crawl! Reflecting on all this, consider nothing to be great, except to act as your nature leads you, and to endure what the common nature brings.
12.33: How does the ruling faculty make use of itself? For everything lies in this. But everything else, whether it is in the power of your will or not, is only lifeless ashes and smoke.
12.34: This thought is the best suited to move us to contempt of death: that even those who think pleasure a good and pain an evil have still despised it.
12.35: The man to whom only that is good which comes in due season, and to whom it is all the same whether he has done more or fewer acts in keeping with right reason, and to whom it makes no difference whether he contemplates the world for a longer or a shorter time—for this man death is not a terrible thing either.
12.36: Man, you have been a citizen in this great state, the world; what difference does it make to you whether it was for five years or three? For what is in keeping with the laws is just for all. Where, then, is the hardship, if it is no tyrant, nor yet an unjust judge, who sends you away from the state, but nature, who brought you into it? It is the same as if a praetor who has hired an actor dismisses him from the stage.—“But I have not finished the five acts, only three of them.”—You are right, but in life three acts are the whole drama; for what makes a complete drama is decided by the one who was once the cause of its making, and now of its undoing: but you are the cause of neither. Depart, then, content, for the one who releases you is content too.
